column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article's list starts Gottfried II of Raabs as burgrave in 1105, but its text says King Conrad III (who reigned from 1138) established the burgraviate; the 1105 date was left out. The 1427 sale of the castle in the entry is not in the article; not repeated.
The article dates the battle AD 83 or 84, as the entry does.

The article has a 'Siege of Carolusborg (1652)' section saying the fort was built in 1652, against 1653 in its own building history and in the entry; the siege was left out. The Portuguese trading post of 1555 at the site was left out, so as not to seem to contradict the entry's 'first built by the Swedes'.
The article gives his bachelor's degree as 1904, at the age of 17; the year was left out.

The article says the judicial bodies left the building in 1993 ('From then until 1993 the ground floor housed the country's judicial bodies'), while the entry says it housed the court of justice until 2011; the date the courts left was left out. The article reports the view that 1580 may record a remodelling of an older house; left out, as the entry gives 1580 as the year it was built.
Present-day access figures and rates by country were left out.

The entry says he fought Ine of Wessex at Woden's Barrow in 715; the article says the Mercians fought there either against the West Saxons under Ine or together with them against an unnamed opponent, possibly the British. The battle was left out.
The article gives his term as legate of Syria as 63 to 65 but has him marching from Syria in 66; the entry says about 63 to 67. The years of his governorship were left out.

The article gives his birth as 11 September 1365; the entry's dates are 1364–1431. The birth date was left out. The entry has Joan of Arc visit him at Nancy; the article says she came on pilgrimage to Saint-Nicolas-de-Port and does not name where they met. The place of the meeting was left out.
The article says Kumarapala ascended the throne in 1043 CE, after Jayasimha's death in 1142: evidently a slip for 1143. No year was given for his accession.
The entry says the treatise defends the alphabet against those who held that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin were fit for Scripture; the article does not give that argument, so it was not repeated.

The article says that 'over the ensuing decade' after 1583 he extended his power to all of Shikoku, which sits awkwardly with Hideyoshi's conquest of 1585 and with the entry's 'most of Shikoku'; the extent of his rule was left out. Popular-culture references (video games) left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: little beyond his titles, his marriage, a list of children and his burial
The article names Ferdinand I as the emperor to whom he paid in 1550, although Charles V reigned until 1556; Ferdinand was named without the imperial title.
The article dates his appointment as bishop to 742 or 748 ('sometime after 742'); the entry gives 742. No year was given for his appointment.
The tables of vowels, consonants and ligatures are empty in the saved article; only the alphabetical order is given.

The article calls Qullasuyu the south-eastern region and places the native Qulla Quechuas mainly around Cochabamba and Potosí; the entry calls it the southern quarter and names the Colla of the Lake Titicaca basin. Neither the direction nor the people's homeland is given in the text. Short article: the text keeps close to its few facts.
The meaning of the name (friend, smiter, or a Gallo-Belgic title) is left out for length.

The entry names Agnes's husband as a son of Henry the Lion; the article does not, so it is not repeated. Heidelberg, Alzey and the lower Neckar are the entry's; the article names only Schönau Abbey near Heidelberg.
The Abbé de Choisy's character sketch and the anecdotes of his rise (the Persian debt, the cannon weighed by boat) are left out for length.

The entry gives material as early as 300 BCE; the article also says the middle of the 1st millennium BCE and mentions Kodumanal (3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE) only as possible evidence. The text gives no early date.

The article contradicts itself on the date of the Xitle eruption and abandonment (245-315 CE, around 400 CE, AD 150-200, and the 1st century BCE) and on the start of the pyramid (a few centuries BCE, or 800-600 BCE). The text gives no date for either; the entry's c. 800 BCE to c. 250 CE stands.

The entry dates the script c. 1550-1050 BCE; the article gives that range and also 1500-1150 BC for its use in the Late Cypriot period. No range is given in the text. The entry says it developed from Linear A and was the ancestor of the Cypriot syllabary; the article says thought to be derived and somehow related, so neither is restated.

The entry says he arrived in the Peloponnese in June 1821 and defended Argos in 1822; the article says he arrived at Hydra in June 1821 and does not mention Argos. The text gives no month for his arrival in the Morea and leaves Argos out.

The article gives the Vimal Vasahi as constructed by 1031 and also as mostly built in 1026; the entry says 1031. The text gives no date for it. The Pittalhar's building dates (1316-1432) look garbled in the article and are left out.
The article dates the compilation to the 3rd-4th century CE; the entry says probably the 4th century. The text gives no date. The entry's ending at the reign of Mahasena is not in the article.
The article says the Polish army prepared an offensive against Denikin's forces in 1920, which looks like a slip for the Soviets; left out.

The article's lead calls Vasily II his nephew; he was his cousin, as the entry says. The text calls him Vasily I's son only. The article places Vasily II's capture outside Suzdal in 1445 and Shemyaka's seizure of Moscow and the blinding right after it; the entry dates the seizure to 1446. The text dates only the capture.

The article treats the campaign as the German capture of the islands; the entry frames it as a British attempt. Both are told without contradiction. Leros's fall date (November) left as in the entry; the article's section gives no exact date.

Short article; the text adds the context, the UN's response, the referendum and his later offices. The article dates the referendum to September and the election to October 1961 in different places, so no month is given.
The article dates the bishopric's founding to 634 (the entry: Birinus baptised Cynegils in 635) and the move of the see to Lincoln to 1085 (the entry: Mercian see until 1072). Both dates left out.

The entry places Doris in the upper valley of the Cephissus; the article describes the valley of its tributary the Pindus, which joins near the Cephissus's sources. Worded so as not to contradict. Much of the article concerns the Dorians at large; only what bears on the region is used.
The article says he helped his son-in-law win the Battle of Chengpu against Chu; left out as the identity of the son-in-law there is unclear.

The article dates the discovery of oil to 1937 and the first well to 1939-1940; the entry says oil was found in 1939. The discovery year is left out. The article gives the distance to Doha as about 80 km in the lead and 84 km under Geography; no figure given.
The lead dates the Roem–Van Roijen Agreement to May 1949, the Background section to 6 July; no day given.

The article says Thepphiphit was exiled for his rebellion of December 1759, but dates the rebellion itself to December 1758; the exile is given without a date. The article makes Ekkathat the 33rd monarch of Ayutthaya; not used.

The entry says Moulay Ismail stripped the palace in the late 17th century; the article cites al-Ifrani's date of 1707-08 for his order while saying the dismantling probably began well before. No date given for the stripping. The 2023 earthquake damage and recent exhibitions left out.

The article contradicts itself on the murder: the killer is a 'rebellious nephew' in one place and 'Emperor Taizong's cousin Yelü Chage' in another, and the death is dated 7 October in the lead and 'a night in September 951' in the text. Neither the killer nor the month is given. The entry's 'defeating the supporters' of the empress dowager is not contradicted: the article says the nobles refused her support. Thin article; the family section adds little.
The article gives his death as c. 1836 BC; the entry dates his reign c. 1860-1837 BCE. No death date given.
Thin article; the text adds his title, the bowl inscriptions, the archaeology of Kish and the succession.
The article is unclear whether the ELF fled to Sudan in 1980 or 1981 (the entry: 1981); no year given for the flight.
The 712 date is given as unconfirmed and is kept as such.

The entry dates the inscriptions between about the 8th and 4th centuries BCE; the article gives the syllabary inscriptions as 6th to 3rd centuries BC (VI-III BC) and the language's extinction about the 4th century BC. The range of the inscriptions is left out.

The article says the captured Alexios V was eventually forced to retire to a monastery; this is left out as doubtful (he is generally said to have been executed) and not needed. The article's infobox wording gives her death as c. 1211 or later; the text keeps 'thought to have died around 1211', as the entry's dates.

The article gives 27 deaths in the battle according to official records, most of them rebels; the entry says about 22 miners were killed. The death toll is left out. Rede's office is not stated in the saved text (its section on the gold commissioner is empty), so he is named without a title.

The article says Caccini published his version before Peri's was performed, in 1600, and also that he rushed to publish after learning of Peri's plans; the text only says Caccini's was published first.
The article gives his death as 1402-1404 (c. 1402/1404); the entry has c. 1402. The year of death is left out of the text.

The entry places the Heysel plateau in the north of the city; the article says 7 km north-west of central Brussels. The direction is left out. Visitor numbers (nearly 42 million in the lead, 41.5 million in the body) are left out as the entry already gives more than 40 million.
The article names the triumvirate twice, once as Ruiz de Alda and once as Julio Ruiz de Alda; the full form is used.
The article says sixty-six paintings went to Poland; the split between Warsaw and Khartoum is left out.
Pollution below the reservoirs, which the article describes as a current problem, is left out.
SKIPPED: The article has about 250 words, almost all on the bombing of the Rainbow Warrior that the description already tells; nothing on Pereira's own life or work.
The article says the building was rebuilt between 1505 and 1508 and that the frescoes date from 1508; consistent with the entry.
The saved article's list of member states is empty, so the composition is told only from the 1500 text and the entry.
The article gives his death as 1131 in its opening line but says he was killed near Valencia in 1130; the entry has 1131. The year of the battle is left out of the text.
SKIPPED: The article has about 200 words of substance (its list of members is not in the saved text) and adds little to the description beyond the origin of the term.
The article says both that he returned after 'a year in exile' and that he lived in Vermont from May to October 1838; the length of exile is left out.

The article says in one place that he abdicated in 1622 before the campaign, to avoid an imperial ban, and in another that he abdicated at Stuttgart after Wimpfen; the timing is left out (the entry says he handed over government to fight). The article's lead says he succeeded in 1604; it also describes him ruling Baden-Hachberg from 1595.

The entry gives the defeat at Chikhori in 1463 and capture in 1465; the article's chronology of the war with Bagrat and Samtskhe is confused (Uzun Hasan's victory 1461, 1462 or 1463; Bagrat's usurpation 1462 in the legacy section, coronation February 1466), so no dates are given for the defeat or the capture. The article says he married Tamar Jaqeli first in the family section but calls that marriage a lesser-known, later forced one in the captivity section; left out.

The article dates A History of the Negro Troops to 1887 in the text and 1888 in the book list; the year is left out. Left out the claim that the Belgian government's takeover followed from his campaign: the article draws the link loosely.

The article gives his birth as 23 March 1903; the entry's dates say 1904. The birth year is left out. The article treats the death as suicide in its narrative but says it is still disputed whether suicide or assassination; the entry says probably suicide. The text says it is disputed without contradicting 'probably'.

The article says both that Baekje established relations with Jin in 345 and that the first contact came in 372; only the 372 mission, which Korean and Chinese sources record, is given. The article's claims of Baekje commanderies in Liaoxi and advances into Kyushu are left out as unsupported in its own text. The article says the capital moved to Hansan (a reform) and the Samguk sagi places the move after 371; no date given.

The article says his birth is given between 1421 and 1429, often as 1426 but perhaps 1429; no birth year given. The entry calls him chief minister under Ferrante; the article does not name Ferrante, so that is not repeated or contradicted.

The article gives her dates as c. 35 BCE to c. 7 CE; the entry dates her to the 1st century BCE. Her birth and death years are left out. The article says the marriage broke the Jewish laws of levirate marriage; the text says only that it broke Jewish law on such unions, as the levirate rule is not explained there.

The article dates the wagon burial of grave 3200 both 'around 2200 BCE' and, by radiocarbon, to 2250 BCE; the entry gives 2250, so no date is repeated here. The article spells one author 'Muhamed A. Mamedovone' (probably a slip for Mamedov); the name is left out.

The article gives conflicting dates for the meeting with William III (11 September or 9 November 1697) and for the crossing to England (sailed 18 January 1698, but arrived 11 January Old Style); these dates are left out.
The entry says Crazy Horse surrendered in 1877 and the US annexed the Black Hills; consistent with the article.

The article names Isabella's husband as Bernardo Sanseverino in one place and Niccolò Bernardino Sanseverino, Prince of Bisignano, in another; neither first name is given. The article spells the son-in-law Frederico Borromeo (usually Federico); kept as the article has it. The entry says Paul III forced him to give up Camerino in 1539; the article does not tell how Camerino was lost, so nothing is said of it.
SKIPPED: article too thin: a list of where they live and three books about them, no history

The entry says he presided over the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948; the article says he was President of the General Assembly 1948-49 and helped draft it. Not contradicted.
The article is about the present ward, Hakata-ku; only its history, setting and lasting facts are used. Left out: cruise traffic, population and company figures, and the 2016 sinkhole.

The entry calls Hamar the administrative centre of Innlandet county; the article says only that it was the principal city of the former Hedmark county and is the centre of Hamar Municipality. That point is left out. The article says the 1815 commission recommended a town at Lillehammer, apparently a slip in the section on Hamar's founding; left out. The article places the move to Domkirkeodden 'presumably after 1030 but clearly before 1152'; the entry dates the bishopric to 1152. Only 'after 1030' is used.
The article calls the Jewish emigration 'the largest migration in history'; left out. The article names Ballin as director general among those involved in its development; the entry gives his role.

The article's lead dates the text 'to the reign of Ramesses III' but later says it was written under Ramesses IV, as the entry has it; only the latter is used. The article's estimates of the temples' share of land are inconsistent (at least one-tenth for Thebes alone, then 14.5% for all temples); the share of the whole land is left out. The article gives 'Birch 1876' without a first name.

The article calls Razan rector of the Shōhei-kō; the entry says the academy he founded in 1630 became the Shōheikō under his descendants. The text names only the hereditary headship and the later name Yushima Seidō.
SKIPPED: different subject: the article is about the empress Helena Kantakouzene (1333-1396), daughter of John VI and wife of John V, not his granddaughter the Countess of Salona
Article says first half of 9th century and probably around 830; consistent with entry c. 830.
Article gives his death as 30 July 1613 in the lead and 20 July 1613 in the body; text says only July 1613.
Article names Pope Alexander VI as granting the 1412 dispensation, an anachronism; the pope is left unnamed. Entry's claim that he imprisoned Louis VII is not in the article; left untouched.
Article names the Cham king of 1402 Jaya Simhavarman V, after calling La Ngai Jaya Simhavarman VI for 1390; names left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: one sentence on Shengle, then data centres, statistics and transport
Article gives his death as 16 September 1910 in the lead and 8 September 1910 later; text says only September 1910.
Article gives 15 January 1938 as death date in the lead but says the exact date is unknown; text gives only that he died in prison.
Article gives his birth as c. 1165, the entry c. 1166; birth year left out.
Article's GDP figures (21.5 to 56.1 percent) are unintelligible and left out; article's economic section is partisan in tone, only plain facts used.
Article's Saint-Joseph 'Reclusion' and dates 1852-1953 are in the entry already.

Article dates his rule of Mardin from 1107 in the lead but says he took Mardin in 1108; text uses only the 1108 seizure. Article names the sultan as Mahmud I for the Baghdad office, which looks doubtful; left unnamed.
Article gives two accounts of the Islamisation: by Dagestani rulers after Elisu's foundation, and via Lezghin and Ottoman influence in the 17th century; text follows the first only.
The Tokaido ferry in the entry is not in the article.
Article questions Schoff's reading that Isidore came from Charax in Characene (charax means palisade and several towns bore the name); the entry states Charax Spasinou, so the point is left out.
Article gives both fewer than 40 fluent speakers and about 1,000 speakers among 2,000; the entry says only a few elderly speakers; no figure given in the text.

The article says Anvelt 'arrived in the USSR' in 1925, after the 1924 coup attempt; the entry says he directed the underground and the 1924 uprising from Soviet Russia. The arrival year is left out so the page does not disagree with itself. The article's October Revolution section concerns Tallinn in November 1917; the entry's Commune of November 1918 in Narva is a separate event and not restated.

The article has no history section; the entry's prehistoric farming, stone walls and Iron Age burial mounds are not in it, so nothing on them is added. Erik the Red is listed among notable people without saying he was born in Jæren; left out.

The article dates the Ashvamedha sacrifices both to 1734 and 1741 and to 1716 (with the Vajapeya in 1734); no dates given for the rites. The article gives the Sawai title both 'before the siege of Vishalgad' and as a reward for the siege of Khelna (1702); the siege is not named. The article says Jaipur 'officially replaced Amber as the capital' by 1733 and the capital moved in 1727; the entry's 1727 founding is not restated.

The 2008 statements of Bruce Golding on homosexuality and Holness's 2022 remarks on a republic referendum are left out for length. The article calls the JLP 'the current governing party'; written as the dated result of the 2025 election only.

The article's lead says 500 British South Africa Company police; its body says around 600 men. The entry says about 600; the total is not restated. Later research on Chamberlain's possible involvement (Graham Bower's Secret History, 2002) left out for length.

The article gives the daughters' birth years as 1603, 1608 and 1610, but also says the first child was born in 1603 by 'Soetken Gaven'; the birth year 1570 is given in both lead (c. 1570) and body (1570). The entry says c. 1570, so no birth year is printed. The article dates the move from Salé back to Algiers to the end of 1627; left out, as the Iceland raid of 1627 is said to sail home to Salé. The entry says 'after 1641'; the article lead says c. 1641 and the body that the date of death is unknown. Last known date August 1641 kept, no death date given.
Kuibishev spelt as the article spells it (usually Kuibyshev).

The entry says Japan captured the concession in 1914; the article says it was occupied by British and Japanese forces after the siege. Written as surrender after a British and Japanese siege, without saying who held it after. The entry's German occupation of 1897 is not in the article.

The article's lead says she was duchess 'until the occupation of the duchy by her brother-in-law Louis II of Flanders' but also that she ruled until her death; the entry's 1355-1406 is kept and the lead's phrase left out.

The article says he married 'two years later' than 1887 'at 38 years old', which do not agree with his birth in 1849; no year or age of the marriage given. The 1905 start of the ambassadorship is in the entry and not repeated.

The entry says he was shot by police while fleeing; the article says he was killed by an askari military patrol. Written as 'tracked down and killed' without saying by whom. The article gives his return to Nyasaland as both 1900 and 1901; no year printed. Whether he preached millenarian ideas is disputed in the article; left out for length.

The article dates his rule as Duke of Bavaria-Munich 'since 1375' and his joint rule 'in Bavaria-Landshut' from 1375; the entry calls it joint rule with his brothers until 1392. Kept as the article's body gives it. Birth year 1341 (entry c. 1341) not printed.
The 1932-33 famine inquiry is given as the article names it, the International Commission of Inquiry into the 1932-33 Famine in Ukraine.

The article says Pym's ideas and language were adapted by Patriots in the American Revolution; left out for length. The expulsion of Henry Marten is told only through one historian's reading (David Como) and left out.

The entry's directorship of the National Library is not in the article. The article's list of Huasipungo editions is muddled ('two more editions ... 1934, 1953, 1960'); written as rewritings in 1953 and 1960.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; little beyond the existing description (exile in Curaçao, defeat at Coplé, death in Martinique)

SKIPPED: article has under 300 words; everything it adds to the description (founding by Samba Taal, the Courland lease of 1651, the 1860s razing and 1866 bombardment, tourism after Roots) comes to about 230 words, below the minimum

The article gives his death as 12 August 1911 in the lead and 13 August 1911 in the body; no day printed. The article also says he and Cazeneuve were at Toba-Fushimi in January 1868, before the mission was recalled, which sits oddly with the later account of leaving Yokohama in October; left out.

The entry says he was elected for the Revolutionary Party; the article does not say so (it names the PR only as a target of Mano Blanca) and the party is not named. The rumour that his cousin's murder had presidential sanction is reported in the article's lead only as a rumour; left out. The March 1966 disappearances fall before his inauguration in July 1966; the article places them in its account of his presidency. Kept as the start of the repression without saying under whom.

The article dates the dynasty's power in Jibal to c. 1008-c. 1051 and calls the later Kakuyids atabegs of Yazd; the entry says the heiresses passed under the atabegs who founded the Atabegs of Yazd. I wrote only that the family governed Yazd and Abarkuh, avoiding the word atabegs. The article's sentence placing Garshasp I's accession 'while in Hamadan' is unclear; I used its ruler list (Garshasp I, Hamadan, 1041-1048).

The article says both that Shahu, through Balaji Vishwanath, made Angre head of the navy by an agreement around 1707, and that the titles came with the 1713 settlement after the capture of the Peshwa. I told only the 1713 settlement. The article dates the Mathews expedition to 29 November 1721 in its narrative and to 1722 (against Kolaba) in its list of battles; I used the narrative date. The article calls him 18 in 1685, which does not fit his birth in 1669; I gave no age. Left out the article's evaluative claims (most skilled Indian navy chief) and the pop-culture tributes.
The article gives his death as 28 February 1942; the entry implies he died on 27 February, the day of the battle. I gave no date for his death.

The article's History section says the place cannot be traced before the 17th century, while its Places of interest section says the Dutch, French and British had trading posts there by the middle of the 16th century. I left the second claim out. The entry calls it a town near Murshidabad; the article calls it a suburban area of Berhampore city in Murshidabad district. I used the article's wording for the present only.

The article gives the fief after Sekigahara as 200,000 koku and says he served for a time as lord of Aizu; the entry says he was moved to Aizu in 1627 with 400,000 koku. Not strictly contradictory; I gave only the article's 200,000 after Sekigahara and no figure for Aizu. Matsuyama Castle is not in the article, so it is not mentioned. The article does not date the incident with Ishida Mitsunari beyond 'after the death of Hideyoshi in 1598'.
The article's account of the union's names before 1946 (KAU, KASU, a ban of parties in 1939) is confused, so I left it out. The article lists Gideon Moi as chairman from 2013 'to present'; not used.

The article's sentence that the sea 'had retreated by about 600ft by 1907' is unclear (shoreline retreat or sea retreat); left out. Left out the oil finds, development projects and the July 2026 floodgate opening as not lasting facts.

The article gives the village 157 inhabitants and the dead as around 149, including 70 or 75 children; the entry speaks of its 149 inhabitants, including 75 children. I gave no population or death figures.

The article does not say where Khumarawayh was killed; the entry says Damascus. I gave no place. The article's dates for the Battle of Tawahin (6 April) imply 885 or 886 without saying which; I gave no date.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: little beyond the entry except the embankment's cherry trees
The article calls the stone carvings soapstone figures and heads and does not use the name pomdo, which is in the entry; not contradictory. The article gives no date for Kissi Kaba Keita's execution.
The article's 'except in the Hopi and Pueblo region' for the change in the ratio is unclear; I wrote 'outside the Hopi region'. Check if the editor prefers to drop it.

The article says the brothers had been Ottoman vassals since the Battle of Maritsa (1371) but also that Ottoman sources report Jovan was compelled to accept vassalage in 1373. I gave no year for the vassalage. Left out the article's claim that three daughters married Murad I and his sons Bayezid and Yakub in 1372; it sits oddly with his known daughter and the dates, and I could not confirm it from the article itself.
The entry spells Messberghof; the article Meßberghof. I used the article's spelling.

The article says the Confucian scholar Zhu Zhiyu helped redesign the garden; he is usually said to have died in 1682, before construction began in 1687, so I left the claim out. The entry says the garden was built for Ikeda Tsunamasa and completed in 1700, which the article also says.

The article calls the fort the third-largest in the Americas in its lead and the second-largest colonial military installation in the New World on completion (after Cartagena); the entry says it was the largest Spanish fortification in the Americas. I gave no ranking. The article gives 176 documented executions at La Cabaña during Che's command (dated 3 January to 26 November 1959) and elsewhere 55 to 105 under his jurisdiction, with his tenure as 2 January to 12 June 1959. I gave no figure and used the 2 January to 12 June dates for his command of the prison.
The Méma region named in the entry is not in the article. The article says the earliest known report of the lake dates from the first millennium BC; I left that vague claim out but kept Ptolemy.

Left out the 2021 statement of the Supreme Indigenous Council of Michoacán and its poverty figures as not lasting facts. The article puts the environmental changes in 'the past 50 years' without dates; I gave none.

The article says the lake was built by a Maharaja of the Parmar Rajputs in 1362, that Banjaras occupied it at the end of the 14th century, that a dam was built for the Banjara to ford the stream, and that Udai Singh built the embankment in 1560 and strengthened the dam 'after 1560'. The entry says a Banjara grain trader dammed the stream and that Udai Singh founded Udaipur in 1559. I named no builder and gave no years for the dam or the founding.

The article also says other evidence suggests the camp dates from the Punic Wars; left out as unsupported. The article dates the separation of Numidia from Africa Vetus to Septimius Severus 'AD 193'; the entry says the governor sat at Lambaesis from around 198. I gave no year for the province.

The entry says Leo briefly held Lublin; the article does not mention Lublin, so it is not touched here. The article's lead gives his death as c. 1301, its body as 1301; the text follows the body and the entry.
The article spells the instrument 'viola de gamba'; written here as viola da gamba.

The article excerpt does not give the year of Yan's destruction (the entry's 913), so no year is given for it here. The excerpt does not say how Li Kening was related to Li Cunxu, so no relationship is given.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it adds only the canal's older names, its designer Shi Lu, its locks and its place on the UNESCO tentative list

The article gives his birth as c. 1835, the entry c. 1845: no birth year is given here. The article puts Mzilikazi's death in 1868; the entry dates Lobengula's succession to 1870. The text gives neither year for the succession. The article's Background section is garbled about the Transvaal; only its plain statements are used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (a short biography and a list of children); the entry already covers most of it

The article gives founding dates from the 8th to the 18th century depending on the historian; the entry says it flourished from about the 16th. The text reports the historians' range without a date of its own.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the entry it adds only the abandonment in 1950, the Rhine–Main–Danube Canal that replaced it and the 60 km that survive
The article spells the region Lauraguais in one place and Louraguais in another; Lauraguais is used, the second omitted.

The article's pre-history says the British 'established the Madras State' around 1801, which confuses it with the Madras Presidency; the text speaks only of British power there. Area and population figures are those before the 1953 split.

The article gives the founding as 1335 from coins but Firishta's date of the revolt as 1340; the entry says 1335. Neither year is printed for the revolt. The article cites Bowman for a conquest in 1370 and also dates the last sultan's death and Vijayanagara's formal possession to 1378 (the entry's date). The 1370 date is left out.

The article is inconsistent on his exile: he was sent to India after the 1919 revolt, 'remained in India until 1922', but also 'arrested and sent into exile to India in 1921'. No exile year is given. The article says he was involved in uprisings until 1932, was captured and exiled to southern Iraq, and staged a brief revolt in May 1941; the entry calls 1930–31 his last rising and says he lived under restriction thereafter. Both the 1932 and 1941 points are left out. The entry says British air power ended his rule by 1924; the article says only that he was king until 1924. Not repeated.
